passage:
Week one: Noor wanted the big paintbox at the stationery shop, the one with twenty-four colours. She had eleven rupees. Her brother Pranav spent his coins on toffees every day and waved the wrappers at her. She nearly gave in on Friday. Instead she dropped her coins into an old tea tin and wrote the price on the lid.
Week three: The tin rattled heavier. At Pranav's birthday party she took one sweet instead of five, and didn't complain when her turn at the carrom board came last.
Week five: Noor tipped out the tin and counted twice. Enough. She carried the paintbox home against her chest like a trophy. 'I waited for this,' she told Pranav. 'All by myself.'

qa.q: Where did Noor keep her coins?
qa.a: In an old tea tin, with the price written on the lid.

qa.q: How did Noor feel carrying the paintbox home, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt proud; she held it against her chest like a trophy and said she had waited all by herself.

qa.q: What choice in week one set up Noor's success?
qa.a: Instead of giving in on Friday, she put her coins in the tea tin and wrote the price on the lid, making her goal visible.

qa.q: How might Pranav see Noor's paintbox after watching her save?
qa.a: Pranav might be impressed, or a little envious, seeing that her waiting brought something bigger than his daily toffees.

grounding: Shows a child saving pocket money and waiting her turn, realising that waiting brings more, and feeling proud of managing it.

passage:
Aparna, you want the tablet game now-now? Let me tell you about your Dada's cricket bat. When I was nine, just little Gurpreet in Ludhiana, a willow bat sat in the shop window near our gali. Eighty rupees. The shopkeeper laughed at me, but he promised to keep it. My pocket money was one rupee a week.
Eighty weeks! I thought I'd die of waiting. So I made a paper chart and coloured one box every Sunday. Some weeks I wanted jalebi so badly I could smell it in my sleep. I didn't buy it.
When the last box was coloured, I ran to the shop with the coins knotted in a handkerchief. Holding that bat, I felt taller than the gurdwara gate.
It broke long ago. But I still remember that pride.

qa.q: How much did the willow bat cost?
qa.a: Eighty rupees.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet feel when he finally held the bat?
qa.a: He felt proud and taller than the gurdwara gate, because he had waited eighty weeks for it.

qa.q: What choice helped young Gurpreet get through eighty weeks?
qa.a: He made a paper chart and coloured one box each Sunday, and turned down jalebi even when he badly wanted it.

qa.q: How might the shopkeeper have seen young Gurpreet when he finally came with the coins?
qa.a: The shopkeeper, who had laughed at first but kept the bat, was probably surprised and impressed that a nine-year-old really saved for eighty weeks.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a child saving pocket money for something he wanted and feeling proud of managing the wait.

passage:
First week of June: Mridul wanted the cricket bat in the sports-shop window. It cost more than he had. He almost spent his pocket money on ice cream as usual, but put it in a steel tin instead. His sister Jaya drew him a chart with twelve boxes.
Middle of July: His friends bought chips after school. Mridul watched, stomach growling, and coloured in another box that evening. Some days it felt endless.
First Sunday of September: The tin was full. At the shop he held the bat, the real one, not the cheap plastic one he could have bought in June. He carried it home under his arm, grinning so wide his cheeks ached.

qa.q: How many boxes did Jaya draw on the chart?
qa.a: Twelve boxes.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel carrying the bat home?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy, grinning so wide his cheeks ached.

qa.q: What helped Mridul keep saving?
qa.a: The steel tin and Jaya's chart, which made his progress visible box by box.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel seeing Mridul with the bat?
qa.a: Jaya likely feels proud of her brother and glad her chart helped.

grounding: Shows over months a child saving pocket money instead of spending it, and the pride of getting something better by waiting.

passage: Sumit, you want everything today. Let me tell you about my red bicycle. When I was ten, in Nagpur, I saw it in Gupta-uncle's shop and wanted it so badly I dreamt about it. My father said, "Save, and I'll add the same." So every coin from Diwali, every coin from my aunts, went into a clay pot. My brother bought kites and sweets and laughed at me. Twice I nearly broke the pot for a film ticket. I, Vasudha, held on for fourteen months. When we finally carried that bicycle home, my brother asked for a ride, and I let him, grandly, like a queen. I've never been so proud of anything I owned.

qa.q: How long did young Vasudha save?
qa.a: Fourteen months.

qa.q: How did young Vasudha feel when the bicycle came home?
qa.a: She felt deeply proud, letting her brother ride grandly, like a queen.

qa.q: What was the hardest choice in the story?
qa.a: Not breaking the pot for a film ticket, twice, which kept the bigger goal alive.

qa.q: How might the brother have felt asking for a ride?
qa.a: He may have felt a bit sheepish after laughing at her, and happy she shared.

grounding: Shows a child learning to delay reward by saving for a bicycle and taking pride in having managed it.

passage: The queue for the giant wheel at the Durga Puja fair was forty minutes long, the evening was sticky, and Anirban's feet hurt. Right beside it, the toy train had no queue at all. "Let's just go on the train," said his friend Siddharth, tugging his sleeve. Anirban looked up at the wheel's lights turning slowly against the dark. Last year he'd have given up. This year he'd waited his turn at the pani-puri stall without once whining, and his mother had noticed. "I'm staying," he said. He and Siddharth played word games to pass the time. When they reached the top of the wheel, the whole fair glittering below, Anirban felt a proud warmth. "Worth it," he whispered.

qa.q: How long was the queue for the giant wheel?
qa.a: Forty minutes long.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel at the top of the wheel?
qa.a: He felt a proud warmth, pleased that his waiting had paid off.

qa.q: What helped Anirban and Siddharth get through the wait?
qa.a: Playing word games to pass the time.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel at the top of the wheel?
qa.a: Siddharth is probably glad they stayed, even though he wanted the train.

grounding: Illustrates a child choosing to wait his turn for a bigger reward and enjoying the pride of managing it.

passage:
Thomas had wanted the remote-control jeep in the window of the toy shop near Malad station since Diwali. It cost more than three months of his pocket money.
Every Sunday, when Papa handed him his coins, Thomas stood at the ice-cream cart for a long moment, then walked on. He dropped the money into an old tea tin and wrote the new total on a strip of tape.
In February his friend Sumit bought a spinning top the day he got money and lost it in a week. Thomas felt a small sting of envy, then looked at the tape.
In April he carried the tin to the shop himself. The shopkeeper counted it twice. Thomas walked home holding the box against his chest, grinning, and told Papa, "I waited, and it was worth it."

qa.q: Where did Thomas keep his saved coins?
qa.a: He dropped them into an old tea tin and wrote the total on a strip of tape.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling as he walked home in April?
qa.a: He felt proud and happy; he was grinning and holding the box to his chest because his waiting had paid off.

qa.q: What helped Thomas keep going through the months?
qa.a: Writing the new total on the tape each week let him see his progress, which made walking past the ice-cream cart easier.

qa.q: How might Papa see Thomas's months of saving?
qa.a: Papa would likely feel proud that Thomas learned for himself that waiting can bring something bigger.

grounding: Thomas saves his pocket money for a toy, learns that waiting brings more, and enjoys the pride of having managed it.
